title: The day the Sun set telegraph wires on fire
sentences: In September 1859, the sky over the Caribbean glowed red and green at midnight.
Hours earlier, astronomer Richard Carrington had watched a blinding flash erupt on the Sun.
A wave of charged particles then slammed into Earth's magnetic field.
Telegraph wires sparked, papers caught fire, and some lines worked with their batteries unplugged.
Back then, the damage stayed small, because the world barely ran on electricity.
Today, a storm that strong could overload power grids and blind satellites for days.
Scientists now watch the Sun around the clock, waiting for the next one.
Would you be ready if the lights went out for a week?

title: What happens when the Sun finally dies
sentences: Every second, the Sun burns through about six hundred million tonnes of hydrogen.
It has done this for four and a half billion years, and it is only middle aged.
In roughly five billion years, the fuel in its core will run low.
The Sun will then swell into a red giant, hundreds of times wider than today.
Mercury and Venus will be swallowed, and Earth's oceans will boil away long before that.
Finally, the Sun will shed its outer layers into a glowing cloud of gas.
What remains will be a white dwarf, about the size of Earth, cooling for trillions of years.
Does that make our time here feel shorter or longer?

title: Mars once had oceans. Where did they go?
sentences: Billions of years ago, Mars may have had rivers, lakes and maybe even an ocean.
NASA rovers have found dried riverbeds, round pebbles and minerals that only form in water.
So what went wrong?
Mars is small, and its core cooled, so its global magnetic field faded away.
Without that shield, the solar wind slowly stripped the atmosphere into space.
With thinner air, the water froze underground or escaped as vapour.
Today, Mars is a frozen desert, but its ice could one day help astronauts survive.
Should humans try to bring water back to Mars?

title: Why Venus became the hottest planet
sentences: Venus is almost the same size as Earth, and it may once have had shallow seas.
Today its surface is hot enough to melt lead, around four hundred and sixty degrees Celsius.
It is even hotter than Mercury, which sits closer to the Sun.
The reason is a runaway greenhouse effect.
As Venus warmed, water evaporated and trapped more heat, which evaporated even more water.
Now its air is mostly carbon dioxide and ninety times heavier than ours.
Venus is a warning about what extreme heat trapping can do to a whole world.
Would you ever visit Venus, even in its cooler clouds?

title: The asteroid that ended the dinosaurs
sentences: Sixty six million years ago, a rock about ten kilometres wide hit what is now Mexico.
It struck at around twenty kilometres per second.
The impact released energy billions of times greater than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima.
Rock was blasted into space and rained back down as burning debris.
Soot filled the sky and blocked sunlight, so plants struggled and food chains collapsed.
About three quarters of all species vanished, including the large dinosaurs.
But small mammals survived, and that opened the path that eventually led to us.
Is NASA's asteroid watch enough to stop the next one?

title: Hiroshima versus the forces of nature
sentences: On the sixth of August 1945, an atomic bomb destroyed Hiroshima and killed tens of thousands of people.
Its blast equalled about fifteen thousand tonnes of TNT.
It changed history, but it did not change the planet's orbit, climate or magnetic field.
Nature works on a far larger scale.
The 1815 Tambora eruption caused a year without a summer across parts of the world.
A single strong hurricane can release more energy than all the world's weapons combined.
The real lasting damage of Hiroshima was human, carried by survivors for generations.
What should we never forget about that day?

title: Why total solar eclipses are a cosmic coincidence
sentences: During a total solar eclipse, day turns to night in a few minutes.
It works because of a stunning coincidence.
The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, and about four hundred times farther away.
So from Earth, both look almost exactly the same size.
That lets us see the Sun's corona, its outer atmosphere, normally hidden by its glare.
But the Moon drifts away about four centimetres every year.
In hundreds of millions of years, it will look too small, and total eclipses will end forever.
Have you ever seen one in person?

title: Voyager is still talking to us from deep space
sentences: In 1977, NASA launched two small spacecraft called Voyager.
They flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, sending back the first close photos.
Each one carries a golden record with sounds, music and greetings from Earth.
Today, both have left the Sun's bubble and entered interstellar space.
Their radio signals take more than twenty hours to reach us.
Their power is fading, and one day they will fall silent.
But they will keep drifting through the galaxy for billions of years.
What would you put on a record for aliens?

title: Saturn is slowly losing its rings
sentences: Saturn's rings look permanent, but they are slowly disappearing.
They are made of billions of pieces of ice, from tiny grains to chunks the size of houses.
NASA's Cassini spacecraft found that ice is raining down into Saturn's atmosphere.
Gravity and the planet's magnetic field pull the particles in, a little at a time.
Some scientists think the rings could be mostly gone in a few hundred million years.
That means we live at a lucky moment to see them at their best.
Would you trade your view of Earth for one of Saturn?

title: Jupiter's giant storm is shrinking
sentences: Jupiter has a storm bigger than Earth that has raged for hundreds of years.
It is called the Great Red Spot, and its winds can top four hundred kilometres per hour.
Old drawings from the eighteen hundreds show it was once far wider.
Today, it is shrinking and becoming rounder.
NASA's Juno spacecraft found the storm reaches hundreds of kilometres deep.
Nobody knows for sure whether it will vanish or keep fighting for centuries.
What would you name the next giant storm?

title: What the James Webb telescope is really seeing
sentences: When you look at a James Webb image, you are looking back in time.
Light from distant galaxies takes billions of years to reach us.
So Webb sees some galaxies as they were shortly after the universe began.
It sees in infrared, which passes through dust that blocks normal light.
That is how it reveals newborn stars hiding inside clouds.
Its giant gold mirror sits a million and a half kilometres from Earth.
Some of these galaxies may already be gone.
Which question should Webb answer next?

title: How Apollo 13 almost didn't come home
sentences: In April 1970, three astronauts were flying to the Moon when an oxygen tank exploded.
Houston, we've had a problem, became one of the most famous lines in history.
The Moon landing was cancelled, and the goal became simply getting home alive.
The crew moved into the small lunar module and used it as a lifeboat.
They rationed water, power and heat while temperatures dropped near freezing.
Engineers on Earth built a fix for carbon dioxide using only items on board.
After four tense days, the capsule splashed down safely in the Pacific.
Would you have the nerve to fly that mission?

title: Earth's magnetic poles have flipped before
sentences: Your compass points north, but that has not always been true.
Deep inside Earth, swirling molten iron creates a magnetic field around the planet.
That field shields us from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.
Rocks on the ocean floor show the poles have swapped places many times.
The last full flip happened about seven hundred and eighty thousand years ago.
A flip takes centuries, and life survived every one we know of.
But today, it could disrupt satellites, navigation and power systems.
Should we be preparing for the next one?

title: Billions of planets have no sun
sentences: Not every planet orbits a star.
Astronomers believe billions of rogue planets wander the Milky Way alone.
Many were likely flung out of their home systems by the gravity of bigger planets.
With no sunlight, their surfaces would be frozen and dark.
Yet some might keep warm oceans under thick ice, heated from inside.
NASA's upcoming Roman telescope is designed to find many of them.
Could life exist on a world with no sun at all?
